title: 'Cells Control Their Size: A Measured Eukaryotic Cell'

generated.pipeline: extract -> Codex draft -> Codex accuracy gate and fix

cards.front: Concentration is an amount divided by {{c1::volume}}.
cards.back: Growth dilutes a substance when its amount does not keep pace with volume.
cards.quote: Many of a cell's processes depend on concentrations: amount divided by volume.

cards.front: For cell volume, 1 femtolitre equals {{c1::1 µm³}}.
cards.quote: cell volumes are given in femtolitres (fL) or cubic micrometres (µm³), and the two are the same

cards.front: In budding yeast, {{c1::Start}} is the point in G1 where the cell commits to copying its DNA and dividing.
cards.quote: Start, the film's green line, is the point in G1 where the cell commits to a full cycle
cards.section: Reading size: the brake that growth dilutes

cards.front: How does Whi5 act as a brake on Start in budding yeast?
cards.back: Whi5 holds back the transcription factor that activates Start genes. As Whi5 concentration falls, this brake weakens.
cards.quote: Whi5 is a protein that holds back the transcription factor (a gene-switching protein) that turns on the genes for Start
cards.section: Reading size: the brake that growth dilutes

cards.front: What single-cell observation supplies the key premise of the Whi5-dilution model?
cards.back: Whi5 was made mostly in S, G2 and M in an amount that hardly depended on cell size, so differently sized daughters began G1 with similar amounts.
cards.quote: Whi5 was made mostly in S, G2 and M, in an amount that hardly depended on the cell's size.
cards.section: Reading size: the brake that growth dilutes

cards.front: Why can a similar Whi5 amount at birth carry information about a budding-yeast daughter's size?
cards.back: The same amount has a higher concentration in a smaller volume. Growth therefore makes small daughters dilute Whi5 farther before Start.
cards.quote: A small daughter therefore began G1 with about as many Whi5 molecules as a larger cell, at a higher concentration.
cards.section: Reading size: the brake that growth dilutes

cards.front: Two budding-yeast daughters inherit about the same Whi5 amount, but one is born smaller. What happens before Start, and why?
cards.back: The smaller daughter tends to remain in G1 and grow longer. Its higher initial Whi5 concentration takes more growth to dilute.
cards.quote: A small daughter therefore began G1 with about as many Whi5 molecules as a larger cell, at a higher concentration.
cards.section: Reading size: the brake that growth dilutes

cards.front: Under the idealized Whi5-dilution model, what happens to size at Start after doubling the newborn Whi5 dose? What happens after deleting WHI5?
cards.back: Doubling the fixed dose doubles threshold volume in the idealized model; real cells become larger, not necessarily twofold. Deleting WHI5 makes cells pass Start small.
cards.quote: Experimentally, adding WHI5 copies made cells larger, though not by a guaranteed twofold amount. Cells lacking Whi5 pass Start small.
cards.section: Reading size: the brake that growth dilutes

cards.front: The budding-yeast sizer is weak and {{c1::noisy}}, so cells pass Start over a range of sizes.
cards.back: A small cell makes up only part of its size shortfall in one G1.
cards.quote: The budding-yeast sizer is weak and noisy: cells pass Start over a range of sizes, though the chance rises as they grow
cards.section: Reading size: the brake that growth dilutes

cards.front: Two newborn fission-yeast cells have different sizes. If both behave as sizers, how do their growth and division sizes compare?
cards.back: The smaller-born cell grows more and the larger-born cell grows less, so they divide at similar sizes.
cards.quote: a cell born small grows more first, a cell born large grows less, and sizes at division come out similar.
cards.section: Reading size: the brake that growth dilutes

cards.front: Why would Whi5 dilution fail as a size ruler if Whi5 amount at birth rose in direct proportion to birth volume?
cards.back: Every daughter would begin at the same Whi5 concentration, independent of size. Growth-induced dilution would then provide no information about birth size.
cards.why: This combines the amount/volume rule with the model's requirement that Whi5 amount not scale with daughter size.
cards.quote: if the dose at birth grew in proportion to birth size, every cell would start at the same concentration
cards.section: Reading size: the brake that growth dilutes

cards.front: Why must a growing cell make more RNA and protein as its volume increases?
cards.back: Reaction rates depend on molecular concentrations. Making RNA and protein roughly in step with volume keeps their concentrations steady.
cards.quote: a growing cell has to make more RNA and protein to keep their concentrations steady.
cards.section: Keeping pace: contents and the nucleus

cards.front: A cell doubles its volume while doubling its total RNA and protein. What happens to their concentrations, and do they signal size?
cards.back: Their concentrations remain steady. Because amount and volume scale together, concentration does not reveal cell size.
cards.quote: the total amount still grows with the cell, but the concentration carries no size signal.
cards.section: Keeping pace: contents and the nucleus

cards.front: Why can Whi5 concentration act as a size signal while bulk RNA and protein concentrations usually cannot?
cards.back: Whi5 amount at G1 birth changes little with size, so growth dilutes it. Bulk RNA and protein usually increase with volume, holding concentration steady.
cards.why: The distinction follows from whether molecular amount keeps pace with volume.
cards.quote: The ruler works because Whi5 does not keep pace; nearly everything else has to.
cards.section: Keeping pace: contents and the nucleus

cards.front: How would size mutants test whether cell size sets fission-yeast nuclear size, and what would the cell-size model predict?
cards.back: Measure nuclear and cell volumes across mutants spanning a wide size range. If cell size sets nuclear size, the nuclear-to-cell volume ratio stays constant.
cards.why: Holding DNA content comparable while varying cell size separates a cell-size rule from a DNA-only rule.
cards.quote: If cell size sets nuclear size, the nuclear-to-cell ratio stays constant as cells get bigger.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: How does repeated DNA replication without division distinguish DNA-based from cell-size-based control of nuclear size?
cards.back: Compare low- and high-DNA cells. A DNA model predicts a relatively larger high-DNA nucleus; a cell-size model predicts the same nuclear-to-cell ratio.
cards.quote: The DNA model predicts a relatively larger nucleus in the high-DNA cells; the cell-size model predicts the same ratio.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Fission yeast kept a nuclear-to-cell volume ratio near 0.08 across a 35-fold size range and from 2C to 32C DNA. What conclusion follows?
cards.back: In fission yeast, nuclear volume tracks cell volume rather than DNA content.
cards.quote: The answer in fission yeast is cell size, probably through something in the cytoplasm.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In growing wild-type fission yeast, the nuclear-to-cell volume ratio is {{c1::0.080 ± 0.013}}.
cards.back: Carry the cell type with this measured share.
cards.quote: Wild-type fission yeast, growing: nuclear-to-cell volume ratio 0.080 ± 0.013
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A V79-S171 cell has volume 710 µm³, nuclear volume 190 µm³, and total mitochondrial volume 37.5 µm³. Calculate both compartment fractions.
cards.quote: Chinese hamster V79-S171 cells, log phase, in culture: mean volume 710 µm³, nucleus 190 µm³, total mitochondria 37.5 µm³
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Treat a 710 µm³ V79 cell as a sphere. What sphere-equivalent radius and diameter does it have?
cards.back: r = [3(710)/(4π)]^(1/3) = 5.53 µm, so the diameter is 11.07 µm, about 11.1 µm.
cards.quote: Treated as a sphere of the same volume, a V79 cell has r³ = 3 × 710 / (4π) = 169.5 µm³
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why should a measured nuclear or mitochondrial volume fraction always be reported with its cell type?
cards.back: Organelle scaling depends on cell type. A fraction measured in one type is real for that type, not a universal fraction.
cards.quote: Each value is real for its own cell; there is no universal nuclear fraction.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: G1-arrested budding-yeast cells grew from about 65 fL to about {{c1::600 fL}} in six hours, and their cytoplasm was diluted.
cards.quote: held in G1, budding-yeast cells grew from about 65 fL to about 600 fL in six hours, and their cytoplasm was diluted.
cards.section: What can fall behind: the genome

cards.front: Enlarged, G1-arrested yeast are also arrested longer. Design a control that separates dilution caused by size from dilution caused by arrest time.
cards.back: Hold control cells for the same time but limit their growth. Dilution only in the enlarged cells supports size, rather than time arrested, as the cause.
cards.why: The control matches arrest duration while changing final size, isolating the variable that differs.
cards.quote: Hold some cells for the same time but let them grow less.
cards.section: What can fall behind: the genome

cards.front: Why might one genome become limiting when a cell grows extremely large?
cards.back: RNA is copied from a fixed set of DNA templates. At very large size, the nuclear DNA appears unable to support transcription for all the cytoplasm.
cards.quote: At very large sizes the nuclear DNA itself appears to become limiting for transcription
cards.section: What can fall behind: the genome

cards.front: If genome copy number limits how much cytoplasm transcription can support, what size trend should cells with extra genome sets show?
cards.back: They should tend to be larger because extra DNA provides more transcription templates. The lesson reports that this trend fits the idea.
cards.quote: Cells that copy their genome without dividing, or carry extra genome sets, tend to be larger, which fits that idea.
cards.section: What can fall behind: the genome

cards.front: For spheres of radius 5 µm and 10 µm, calculate surface area, volume, and surface-to-volume ratio.
cards.back: At 5 µm: A = 314.2 µm², V = 523.6 µm³, A/V = 0.6 µm⁻¹. At 10 µm: 1256.6 µm², 4188.8 µm³, 0.3 µm⁻¹.
cards.quote: For its sphere going from 5 to 10 µm in radius, A = 314.2 → 1256.6 µm² and V = 523.6 → 4188.8 µm³
cards.section: What falls behind: the surface

cards.front: For a sphere of radius r, the surface-to-volume ratio is {{c1::3/r}}.
cards.back: It falls as radius increases.
cards.quote: For a sphere A/V = 3/r, so 3/r ≥ q/J, which gives r ≤ 3J/q.
cards.section: What falls behind: the surface

cards.front: A spherical cell takes up nutrient at J = 15 molecules µm⁻² s⁻¹ and uses it at q = 9 molecules µm⁻³ s⁻¹. Above what radius can uptake no longer meet demand?
cards.back: Set J(4πr²) ≥ q(4πr³/3). This gives r ≤ 3J/q = 3(15)/9 = 5 µm, so uptake fails above 5 µm.
cards.quote: Supply meets demand when J × A ≥ q × V, with A = 4πr² and V = 4πr³/3.
cards.section: What falls behind: the surface

cards.front: For a spherical cell, J = 20 and q = 6 give r_max = 10 µm. If q doubles while J stays fixed, what are the new r_max and capacity-to-demand ratio at 10 µm?
cards.back: r_max = 3(20)/12 = 5 µm. At 10 µm, capacity/demand = 5/10 = 0.5, so uptake supplies only half of use.
cards.quote: Doubling demand moves r_max exactly as halving uptake would.
cards.section: What falls behind: the surface

cards.front: Why is the spherical uptake calculation a scaling cost rather than a universal maximum cell size?
cards.back: Its limit changes with uptake rate, demand, and shape. Real growth-to-division control chooses size within those costs.
cards.quote: Change J, q or the shape and the answer changes.
cards.section: What falls behind: the surface

cards.front: At equal volume and uptake properties, how should a long thin cell compare with a sphere in nutrient capacity and diffusion distance?
cards.back: The long thin cell should retain more surface per volume and keep points nearer the surface, easing both uptake and diffusion costs.
cards.why: This applies the lesson's surface-to-volume rule and its rule that diffusion time rises with distance squared.
cards.quote: A flat or long thin cell keeps much more surface per volume than a sphere
cards.section: What falls behind: the surface

cards.front: In Arabidopsis root epidermis, the vacuole fills about 30–40% of young cells and {{c1::80–90%}} after elongation.
cards.quote: the vacuole fills about 30 to 40% of young cells and 80 to 90% after elongation.
cards.section: Plants add volume mostly as vacuole, not cytoplasm

cards.front: A plant cell grows from 1,000 µm³ with a 35% vacuole to 10,000 µm³ with an 85% vacuole. By what factor does volume outside the vacuole grow?
cards.back: Initial outside volume = 0.65(1000) = 650 µm³. Final = 0.15(10000) = 1500 µm³. The factor is 1500/650 = 2.31, about 2.3-fold.
cards.quote: Across that comparison the cells grew about 14-fold in volume, while the space between vacuole and cell boundary grew only about two- to threefold.
cards.section: Plants add volume mostly as vacuole, not cytoplasm

cards.front: A spherical plant cell grows 14-fold in volume while its cytoplasm grows only two- to threefold. How do membrane area per total volume and per cytoplasm change?
cards.back: Area grows 14^(2/3) = 5.81-fold. Area per total volume becomes 5.81/14 = 0.415, about 0.4; area per cytoplasm rises about 1.9- to 2.9-fold.
cards.why: A vacuole adds total volume without requiring an equal increase in cytoplasm, changing which denominator matters.
cards.quote: A sphere's area grows as its volume to the power two-thirds, so a 14-fold rise in volume gives 14^(2/3) ≈ 5.8-fold more area.
cards.section: Plants add volume mostly as vacuole, not cytoplasm

cards.front: The fluid outside organelles but inside the plasma membrane is the {{c1::cytosol}}.
cards.back: The space inside an organelle is its lumen.
cards.quote: The space inside an organelle is its lumen; the fluid outside the organelles but inside the plasma membrane is the cytosol.
cards.section: Same parts, different shares

cards.front: Animal, plant, and fungal cells all share a plasma membrane, nucleus, and {{c1::cytoskeleton}}.
cards.back: They also share ER, Golgi apparatus, and mitochondria.
cards.quote: Animal, plant and fungal cells share a plasma membrane, a nucleus and a cytoskeleton
cards.section: Same parts, different shares

cards.front: How do typical animal, plant, and fungal cells differ in walls, plastids, and vacuoles?
cards.back: Animals lack walls and plastids and have small or absent vacuoles. Plants have cellulose-rich walls, plastids, and often large vacuoles. Fungi have walls, no plastids, and acidic vacuoles.
cards.quote: The differences are where students slip
cards.section: Same parts, different shares

cards.front: A root cell deep in soil contains no chloroplasts. Does that observation argue that it is not a plant cell? Why?
cards.back: No. Chloroplasts occur in photosynthetic cells; a nonphotosynthetic root cell can be a plant cell without them.
cards.quote: A root cell deep in soil is a plant cell without them.
cards.section: Same parts, different shares

cards.front: How do a sizer and an adder differ in correcting a cell's birth-size error?
cards.back: A sizer can correct the error within one cycle. An adder adds a similar volume each cycle, so the error shrinks over several generations.
cards.quote: A sizer can correct a size error within one cycle. An adder adds about the same volume each cycle whatever the birth size
cards.section: Sizers, adders and timers

cards.front: What uncertainty should accompany the Whi5-dilution model of budding-yeast size control?
cards.back: It is the leading model, not a closed case; measurements disagree about how far Whi5 concentration falls during G1 and how much size control it explains.
cards.quote: Whi5 dilution is the leading model, not a closed case
cards.section: Debates over what is measured

cards.front: A human ortholog restores growth when substituted for an essential yeast gene. What does this result show, and what does it not show?
cards.back: It shows that the human gene supplies the function yeast needs for growth. It does not establish all human tissue roles or prove failed orthologs lack conserved functions.
cards.quote: That shows a conserved function in those genes. It does not show that the rest are unconserved
cards.section: Model organisms and the limits of transfer

cards.front: Why should findings from a cultured mammalian cell line be reported with the strain and conditions?
cards.back: A cell line is not an animal, and strains bearing the same line name can diversify genetically and respond differently.
cards.quote: Cultured mammalian lines give precise numbers, like the V79 volumes, but a line is not an animal, and a line's name is not a guarantee.
cards.section: Model organisms and the limits of transfer
